articles.title: Positron 2026.10 ships an IDE-wide MCP server: 5 guardrails before Claude Code gets your consoles
articles.excerpt: Posit shipped Positron 2026.10 on November 4 with an experimental feature they call the Positron MCP. Flip one setting, MCP: Enabled, and the IDE starts a Model Context Protocol server that any agent…
articles.body: Posit shipped Positron 2026.10 on November 4 with an experimental feature they call the Positron MCP . Flip one setting, MCP: Enabled , and the IDE starts a Model Context Protocol server that any agent harness can connect to. Posit has tested it with Claude Code (extension and CLI), Codex (extension and CLI), OpenCode, Kiro, Gemini, and Copilot CLI. The pitch is real session awareness. Without the MCP, an agent inside Positron behaves like an agent in a plain terminal: it cannot see your data, your consoles, or your plots, and any R or Python it runs goes through shell commands you watch after the fact. With the MCP on, the agent sees your loaded data, reads your consoles, runs code in them, and can pick up work you started. I have not enabled it against a live session yet.
articles.author: Piekwerk

articles.title: 5 myths about self-hosted uptime monitoring (from someone who ran it on the same VPS)
articles.excerpt: Self-hosting a monitoring tool is a rite of passage. You spin up a container, add your sites, get a nice dashboard with green bars, and feel in control. Open-source monitors are genuinely good, and pl…
articles.body: Self-hosting a monitoring tool is a rite of passage. You spin up a container, add your sites, get a nice dashboard with green bars, and feel in control. Open-source monitors are genuinely good, and plenty of people run them well. But there are a few beliefs about self-hosted monitoring that sound right and cause real gaps. Here are five, with fixes. Myth 1: "Running the monitor on the same server is fine" This is the big one. If your monitor lives on the same VPS as your app, what happens when the VPS goes down? The monitor goes down too. No alert is sent, because the thing that sends alerts is off. Your dashboard shows a gap, which you see when you log in later, after customers have already told you.

articles.excerpt: "How often should we check?" is one of the first questions anyone setting up uptime monitoring asks. The usual answers are opinions: "every minute is standard", "30 seconds if you're serious", "5 minu…
articles.body: "How often should we check?" is one of the first questions anyone setting up uptime monitoring asks. The usual answers are opinions: "every minute is standard", "30 seconds if you're serious", "5 minutes is fine for a blog". Instead of another opinion, let's compare the options with a simulation you can run yourself. It won't give you a universal answer, but it makes the trade-offs concrete: detection delay, missed short outages and the number of requests you'll send. Note: all numbers below come from the simulation with the parameters shown. They're illustrative, not measurements of real sites. Change the inputs to match your situation.

articles.title: Why Does My Phone Camera's Live Stream Stop After a Few Hours on Mobile Data? The 1.5 GB/Day Limit and the 64 Kbps Speed After It
articles.excerpt: You set up an old phone as a camera for the shop or the house. It streams to YouTube Live over a prepaid SIM. It works in the evening. By the early morning the stream is frozen or gone, but the phone…
articles.body: You set up an old phone as a camera for the shop or the house. It streams to YouTube Live over a prepaid SIM. It works in the evening. By the early morning the stream is frozen or gone, but the phone is still on, still charging, and the data icon still shows 4G. On many prepaid plans the reason is the daily data limit . On a plan that says "1.5 GB/day", the data does not stop when the 1.5 GB is used. It gets slow . This guide explains what that means for a phone camera, how many hours of streaming a daily pack really covers, and how to set up the camera so the important hours are not the ones that get cut. It is written for budget and older Android phones on prepaid data, the usual setup in India, Bangladesh and many other markets.

articles.title: HAProxy 503 “No Server Available”: A Practical Debugging Checklist
articles.excerpt: A 503 Service Unavailable from HAProxy usually means HAProxy couldn’t find any usable backend server to send the request to. The right fix depends on why HAProxy considers the backend pool unavailable…
articles.body: A 503 Service Unavailable from HAProxy usually means HAProxy couldn’t find any usable backend server to send the request to. The right fix depends on why HAProxy considers the backend pool unavailable—common reasons include failed health checks, connection refusals/timeouts, queue overload, routing/ACL gaps, or servers being put into MAINT/DRAIN mode. This article lays out a practical troubleshooting workflow: start with the logs , confirm backend state via the stats socket , then resolve the specific failure pattern. What a HAProxy 503 typically looks like From the client side, the error is usually a plain message like: 503 Service Unavailable No server is available to handle this request.

articles.title: Running Qwen3.6 Locally on a MacBook: oMLX + opencode, Faster Than I Expected
articles.excerpt: One 14-inch MacBook Pro. No internet, no API bill. Chat and coding both work, and token output is fast. Load Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (MLX 4bit) locally with oMLX. It is good enough for everyday chat and codin…
articles.body: One 14-inch MacBook Pro. No internet, no API bill. Chat and coding both work, and token output is fast. Load Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (MLX 4bit) locally with oMLX . It is good enough for everyday chat and coding. For chat, just use the built-in web Chat of oMLX. No other client needed. For coding, use opencode and point it at the local oMLX server. Output is fast: roughly 100 tokens/s , estimated from the token counter in my screen recording (details below). Simple tasks and text-heavy tasks (translation, for example) can be handed to it, which can save a lot of API cost. There are two costs. First, memory: the model takes close to 20GB, so a 48GB machine runs it comfortably, but watch the headroom. Second, while a task is running the GPU hits 100%, the fans spin up, and there is some noise.

articles.excerpt: A nasty Chrome bug let hackers break into Android phones without a tap.
articles.body: TL;DR A security firm has found that hackers exploited a Chrome bug and a Qualcomm Adreno GPU driver flaw to infect Android phones that visited a booby-trapped website. The attack targeted Chrome versions 139 to 145 on Android and stole browser cookies, saved logins, browsing history, and Wi-Fi passwords. Both flaws had already been patched, so phones running up-to-date Chrome and security updates remained safe. Security researchers at Sekoia have detailed a mobile hacking campaign that went after Android and iPhone users through hijacked and fake websites. On Android, the attackers didn’t need victims to tap a link, install an app, or grant a permission. Opening an infected page in an outdated version of Chrome was enough.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force launched an experimental Super Strypi rail-launched rocket carrying 13 tiny satellites, but it failed just after liftoff from Hawaii.
articles.body: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms.

articles.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.excerpt: Researchers say group may have been Kremlin-sponsored in search of diplomatic targets.
articles.body: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.
